blocks.text: **The problem.** A **peak** is a value strictly bigger than its neighbours. Given an array `nums` where no two neighbours are equal, return the index of **any** peak. Imagine `nums[-1]` and `nums[n]` are **−∞**, so a value at either end only needs to beat its one neighbour. Your algorithm must run in **O(log n)** time.

blocks.alt: 1, 2, 1, 3, 5, 6, 4 drawn as bars. There are two peaks: 2 at index 1 and 6 at index 5; either answer is accepted. Binary search checks index 3: 3 is less than its right neighbour 5, so climbing right must reach a peak. Then index 5: 6 is more than 4, so a peak is at 5 or to its left. Then index 4: 5 is less than 6, so go right. Only index 5 is left.

elements.text: uphill to the right? a peak must be up there. downhill? one is here or to the left
elements.originalText: uphill to the right? a peak must be up there. downhill? one is here or to the left

blocks.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 1]           ->  2
nums = [1, 2, 1, 3, 5, 6, 4]  ->  5   (or 1)
nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]   ->  4   (always rising: the last value is a peak)

blocks.text: Stand at `mid` and look right. If `nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1]`, the ground rises to the right. Keep walking right: either it keeps rising until the end — and the last value is a peak, because `nums[n]` is −∞ — or it falls somewhere, and the top before the fall is a peak. Either way **a peak exists to the right**, so drop the left half. If instead `nums[mid] > nums[mid + 1]`, the same argument walking left says a peak is at `mid` or to its left. The array isn't sorted and has many peaks, but each comparison still safely throws away half.
**Time O(n), space O(1).** Why is the first downhill step a peak? Everything before it was rising, so `nums[i]` is also bigger than `nums[i - 1]`.
2. Binary search toward the higher side

blocks.caption: Compare mid with its right neighbour and move toward the higher side.

blocks.text: **Time O(log n), space O(1).** The range `low..high` always contains a peak, and it shrinks every step, so when one index is left, it's a peak. (In JavaScript, `(low + high) / 2` is safe; in Java and C++ use `low + (high - low) / 2`.)

blocks.alt: Linear scan: O(n) time, O(1) space. Binary search: O(log n) time, O(1) space.

items: **Always rising / always falling** — the last / first index.
**Several peaks** — any one of them is a correct answer, so test by checking the returned index is a peak, not by comparing with one expected index.
**Extreme values** — `[-2147483648]` or values next to `INT_MIN`: compare neighbours, never add them.
**Peak Index in a Mountain Array** — exactly one peak (previous lesson).
**Find a Peak Element II** — a peak in a 2D grid: binary search the columns, taking each column's maximum, in O(m log n).
**Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array** — the same "which side is safe?" reasoning on a rotated array (Pattern 3).
